apmo-2006-01.title: Triangle inequality and extremal examples
apmo-2006-01.body:
**$n$ even.** Take all $a_i=\frac12$: the sum $\frac n2$ is an integer and every $|a_i-\frac12|=0$. So no positive value works, and $f(n)=0$ (which trivially has the property).

**$n$ odd.** *The value $\frac1{2n}$ works.* Suppose $|a_i-\frac12|<\frac1{2n}$ for all $i$. Since $\sum a_i$ is an integer and $\frac n2$ is a half-integer, $\left|\sum a_i-\frac n2\right|\ge\frac12$. But
$$\left|\sum_{i=1}^n a_i-\frac n2\right|\le\sum_{i=1}^n\left|a_i-\frac12\right|<n\cdot\frac1{2n}=\frac12,$$
a contradiction.

*Nothing larger works.* Let $n=2m+1$ and $a_i=\frac{m}{2m+1}$ for all $i$. Then $\sum a_i=m$ is an integer and
$$\left|a_i-\frac12\right|=\frac12-\frac m{2m+1}=\frac1{2(2m+1)}=\frac1{2n}$$
for every $i$, so no $i$ has $|a_i-\frac12|\ge f$ for any $f>\frac1{2n}$.

**Answer:** $f(n)=0$ if $n$ is even, $f(n)=\dfrac1{2n}$ if $n$ is odd.

apmo-2006-02.title: Induction with the Fibonacci identity
apmo-2006-02.body:
We use $\tau^2=\tau+1$, i.e. $\tau^{k}=\tau^{k-1}+\tau^{k-2}$ for every integer $k$. A *representation* of $N$ is a finite set $E$ of integers with $N=\sum_{e\in E}\tau^e$.

$1=\tau^0$. Assume $N$ has a representation $E$; we construct one of $N+1$.

**Step 1: no two consecutive exponents.** If $E$ contains two consecutive integers, let $k$ be the largest integer with $k,k+1\in E$. Then $k+2\notin E$ (otherwise $k+1,k+2\in E$ contradicts maximality), so we may replace $\tau^k+\tau^{k+1}$ by $\tau^{k+2}$. This keeps the exponents distinct and reduces their number by one, so after finitely many steps $E$ has no two consecutive elements.

**Step 2: free the exponent $0$.** If $0\notin E$, then $E\cup\{0\}$ represents $N+1$. If $0\in E$, let $j\ge0$ be largest with $0,-2,-4,\dots,-2j\in E$; so $-2j-2\notin E$, and since $E$ has no consecutive elements, $-1,-3,\dots,-2j-1\notin E$. Applying $\tau^{-2i}=\tau^{-2i-1}+\tau^{-2i-2}$ repeatedly,
$$\tau^0=\tau^{-1}+\tau^{-2}=\tau^{-1}+\tau^{-3}+\tau^{-4}=\dots=\tau^{-1}+\tau^{-3}+\dots+\tau^{-2j-1}+\tau^{-2j-2}.$$
So
$$E'=(E\setminus\{0\})\cup\{-1,-3,\dots,-2j-1,-2j-2\}$$
is again a set of distinct exponents (the new ones are not in $E$) representing $N$, and $0\notin E'$. Then $E'\cup\{0\}$ represents $N+1$.

By induction every positive integer is a finite sum of distinct integral powers of $\tau$. (For example $2=\tau+\tau^{-2}$, $3=\tau^2+\tau^{-2}$.) ∎

apmo-2006-03.title: A polynomial modulo $p$
apmo-2006-03.body:
There are $\binom{p^2}{p}$ placements, and exactly $p$ of them have all checkers in one row, so
$$r=\binom{p^2}{p}-p=p\left[\binom{p^2-1}{p-1}-1\right],\qquad\text{using }\binom{p^2}{p}=\frac{p^2}{p}\binom{p^2-1}{p-1}.$$
So we must show $\binom{p^2-1}{p-1}\equiv1\pmod{p^4}$. Let
$$f(x)=(x-1)(x-2)\cdots(x-(p-1))=x^{p-1}+s_{p-2}x^{p-2}+\dots+s_1x+s_0 .$$
Then $s_0=(-1)^{p-1}(p-1)!=(p-1)!$ and
$$\binom{p^2-1}{p-1}=\frac{(p^2-1)(p^2-2)\cdots(p^2-(p-1))}{(p-1)!}=\frac{f(p^2)}{(p-1)!}.$$
Since $p\nmid(p-1)!$, it suffices to prove $f(p^2)\equiv s_0\pmod{p^4}$. As $f(p^2)-s_0=s_1p^2+s_2p^4+\dots$, it suffices to show $p^2\mid s_1$.

**$p\mid s_i$ for $1\le i\le p-2$.** By Fermat, $1,2,\dots,p-1$ are $p-1$ distinct roots of $x^{p-1}-1$ over $\mathbb F_p$, so $f(x)\equiv x^{p-1}-1$ coefficientwise modulo $p$.

**$p^2\mid s_1$.** Substituting $x=p$: $f(p)=(p-1)(p-2)\cdots1=(p-1)!=s_0$, so
$$0=f(p)-s_0=p^{p-1}+s_{p-2}p^{p-2}+\dots+s_2p^2+s_1p .$$
Every term except $s_1p$ is divisible by $p^3$: $p^{p-1}$ because $p-1\ge4$, and $s_ip^i$ ($2\le i\le p-2$) because $p\mid s_i$. Hence $p^3\mid s_1p$, i.e. $p^2\mid s_1$.

Therefore $\binom{p^2-1}{p-1}\equiv1\pmod{p^4}$ and $p^5\mid r$. ∎

apmo-2006-04.title: Tangent length of circles tangent to the circumcircle
apmo-2006-04.body:
Let $R$ be the radius of circle $O$ (also writing $O$ for its centre), and let $A,B,C$ also denote the angles of triangle $ABC$, with $a=BC$, $c=AB$.

**Lemma.** Let $V$ be a vertex of triangle $ABC$ and let $\omega$ be a circle inside angle $V$ touching both sides at distance $d$ from $V$, with centre $Z$ on the bisector, $VZ=z=\frac{d}{\cos(V/2)}$ and radius $\rho=z\sin\frac V2$. Then $OZ=|R-\rho|$ (i.e. $\omega$ is tangent to circle $O$) if and only if $z\cos^2\frac V2=4R\sin\frac{V'}2\sin\frac{V''}2$, where $V',V''$ are the other two angles.

*Proof.* The bisector from $V$ meets circle $O$ again at the midpoint $W$ of the arc opposite $V$. For $V=A$, the inscribed angle at $B$ gives $\angle ABW=B+\frac A2=90^\circ+\frac{B-C}2$, so $L=AW=2R\sin\angle ABW=2R\cos\frac{B-C}2$; similarly for any vertex. The power of $Z$ (on line $VW$, at signed distances $-z$ and $L-z$ from $V$ and $W$) is
$$OZ^2-R^2=z(z-L).$$
Since $\sin\frac V2=\cos\frac{V'+V''}2$, we have $L-2R\sin\frac V2=2R\left(\cos\frac{V'-V''}2-\cos\frac{V'+V''}2\right)=4R\sin\frac{V'}2\sin\frac{V''}2$. Then
$$OZ^2-(R-\rho)^2=z^2-zL+2Rz\sin\tfrac V2-z^2\sin^2\tfrac V2=z\left(z\cos^2\tfrac V2-4R\sin\tfrac{V'}2\sin\tfrac{V''}2\right),$$
which proves the lemma.

**$O_1$.** $P$ lies inside circle $O$ and on $O_1$, so $O_1$ is internally tangent to $O$ and lies inside it. Let $X$ be the point where $\ell$ touches $O_1$; then $AX=AP=\frac c2$ and $X$ is inside circle $O$ (it cannot be the tangency point of $O_1$ and $O$, since a line through $A$ cannot be tangent to circle $O$ at another point). So the second intersection $C$ of line $AX$ with circle $O$ lies on ray $AX$ beyond $X$. Hence $O_1$ lies inside angle $BAC$ and touches its sides at distance $d=\frac c2$ from $A$. By the lemma, with $z\cos\frac A2=d$:
$$\frac c2\cos\frac A2=4R\sin\frac B2\sin\frac C2 .$$
With $c=2R\sin C=4R\sin\frac C2\cos\frac C2$ this gives
$$\cos\frac A2\cos\frac C2=2\sin\frac B2 .\tag{1}$$

**$O_2$.** $O_2$ touches line $BC$ at $Q$ and touches segment $AC$, so it lies on $A$'s side of $BC$, inside angle $ACB$, and (equal tangents from $C$) touches both sides at distance $d=CQ=\frac a2$ from $C$. By the lemma at vertex $C$, $O_2$ is tangent to circle $O$ iff
$$\frac a2\cos\frac C2=4R\sin\frac A2\sin\frac B2 .$$
With $a=4R\sin\frac A2\cos\frac A2$ this is $\cos\frac A2\cos\frac C2=2\sin\frac B2$, which is (1). So $OO_2=|R-\rho_2|$, and since $O_2$ is not circle $O$ itself ($O_2$ is tangent to line $BC$, circle $O$ is not), the two circles are tangent. ∎

apmo-2006-05.title: Double counting and a construction
apmo-2006-05.body:
**Upper bound.** Count pairs (clown, colour used by the clown). Each clown uses at least $5$ colours, and each of the $12$ colours is used by at most $20$ clowns, so
$$5n\le\#\text{pairs}\le12\cdot20=240,\qquad n\le48 .$$

**Construction with $48$ clowns.** Group the colours into six pairs $P_1=\{1,2\}$, $P_2=\{3,4\}$, $P_3=\{5,6\}$, $P_4=\{7,8\}$, $P_5=\{9,10\}$, $P_6=\{11,12\}$ and form eight $6$-sets as unions of three pairs:
$$P_1P_2P_3,\ P_2P_3P_4,\ P_3P_4P_5,\ P_4P_5P_6,\ P_5P_6P_1,\ P_6P_1P_2,\ P_1P_3P_5,\ P_2P_4P_6 .$$
Each pair $P_k$ occurs in exactly four of these $6$-sets. Give the clowns all $5$-element subsets of these $6$-sets: $8\cdot6=48$ clowns, each using $5$ colours.
- They are distinct: two different $6$-sets share at most two pairs, i.e. at most $4$ colours, so they have no common $5$-subset.
- A colour lying in a $6$-set belongs to $5$ of its six $5$-subsets, and each colour lies in exactly four $6$-sets, so each colour is used by $4\cdot5=20$ clowns.

**Answer:** $n=48$.
